title: The proem sonnet and its translator
greek: Voi ch'ascoltate in rime sparse il suono
short: Petrarch's opening sonnet, written late as a preface to the whole collection, here in the eighteenth-century version of Lord Charlemont.
body: This is Rerum vulgarium fragmenta 1, the sonnet Petrarch set at the head of his Italian lyrics. It was not written first: it is usually dated about 1350, more than twenty years after he first saw Laura in 1327, when he began arranging the poems into an ordered book. It therefore looks back on the whole love story as a past error. The archive's text comes from the Bohn collection of 1879, which prints it as 'Sonnet I (In Life)' and signs it 'Charlemont', that is, James Caulfeild, first Earl of Charlemont (1728-1799), the Irish statesman, who had spent years in Italy. Bohn's headings ('He Confesses the Vanity of His Passion') are the Victorian editors', not Petrarch's. Charlemont keeps the Italian rhyme scheme, ABBAABBA CDECDE, which few English translators of his period attempted.

title: rhymes dispersed
short: Translates rime sparse, 'scattered rhymes', the phrase that gave the collection one of its names.
body: Petrarch's 'rime sparse' means poems written at scattered moments and kept as separate pieces. His own Latin title for the book, Rerum vulgarium fragmenta ('fragments of things in the vernacular'), makes the same point. Modern readers often call the collection the Rime sparse after this line (Durling's translation is so titled). The paradox is that the proem gathers the fragments into a single designed book while calling them scattered; the sonnet itself is the act of gathering. Charlemont's 'dispersed' is a close, almost Latinate equivalent of 'sparse', and keeps the sense of things strewn about, though not the hint of the scattered limbs of a broken self that some critics hear in it.

title: the echoes hear
short: Petrarch has only 'il suono', the sound; the translator adds 'echoes', making the reader hear sighs repeated long after they were breathed.
body: The Italian addresses those who 'listen in scattered rhymes to the sound' of the sighs. Charlemont turns the sound into 'echoes', which suits the retrospective frame: the reader hears, in written verse, the after-sound of feelings that are now over. The image also anticipates the end of the poem, where the whole experience is dismissed as a dream. The opening address to an audience ('Voi') is itself significant: the poet imagines a public of fellow-lovers who will judge him, and the sestet turns on what that public has said about him.

title: my heart I fed
short: Translates 'di ch'io nudriva 'l core': the lover fed his heart on sighs, a paradox of nourishment by grief.
body: Petrarch's verb nudrire (to nourish) makes sorrow the food of the heart, an image that runs through the collection, where the lover feeds on pain and tears. It is part of the Petrarchan habit of paradox: what should starve the lover keeps him alive. Charlemont translates the line closely. Compare Rvf 134, where Wyatt's 'I feede in sorrow' renders 'Pascomi di dolor'.

title: mazy wanderings
short: Renders 'giovenile errore', youthful error; the Italian word means both wandering and moral mistake, and Charlemont keeps the wandering.
body: Petrarch writes 'in sul mio primo giovenile errore', 'at the time of my first youthful error'. Italian errore, like Latin error (from errare, to wander), means both a straying path and a fault. Charlemont's 'mazy wanderings' brings out the literal, labyrinthine sense, while the poem's later 'repentance' supplies the moral one. Commentators connect the confessional language here with Augustine's Confessions, which Petrarch read closely, and with his Latin dialogue the Secretum, in which 'Augustinus' rebukes 'Franciscus' for his love of Laura.

anchor: Fondly diverse from what I now appear
title: Fondly diverse
short: Petrarch says he was then 'in part another man'; Charlemont adds 'fondly', in its old sense of foolishly.
body: The Italian line is 'quand'era in parte altr'uom da quel ch'i' sono', 'when I was in part another man from the one I am'. The phrase 'in parte' is carefully modest: Petrarch does not claim to be wholly converted, and many critics stress that the collection never fully abandons Laura. Charlemont drops the qualification and adds 'Fondly', which in eighteenth-century usage still carried its older sense of 'foolishly' (OED, fondly, adv., sense 1) as well as 'affectionately'. 'Diverse' means simply 'different'. The change slightly hardens the speaker's judgement on his younger self.

anchor: Fluttering 'twixt frantic hope and frantic fear
title: frantic hope and frantic fear
greek: fra le vane speranze e 'l van dolore
short: Charlemont's doubled 'frantic' imitates Petrarch's doubled 'vane... van' in 'fra le vane speranze e 'l van dolore'.
body: Petrarch's line 6 sets 'vain hopes' against 'vain sorrow', repeating the adjective. Charlemont answers with a repeated adjective of his own, but changes its sense: 'vain' (empty, futile) becomes 'frantic' (frenzied), and 'sorrow' becomes 'fear'. The hope-and-fear pairing is one of the stock antitheses of Petrarchan love, given full treatment in Rvf 134 ('I feare and hope'). 'Fluttering' is the translator's addition and suggests a trapped bird or an unstable heart.

title: my various style
greek: vario stile in ch'io piango et ragiono
short: Translates 'del vario stile in ch'io piango et ragiono': the varied style in which the poet weeps and reasons.
body: Petrarch announces two modes, lament (piangere) and reflection (ragionare), and a 'varied' style: the collection mixes sonnets, canzoni, sestine, ballate and madrigals, and moves between joy, despair, praise and penitence. Variety (varietas) was a positive rhetorical value, and Petrarch's arrangement deliberately alternates forms and moods. Charlemont keeps 'various style' but loses the weeping-and-reasoning pair. In the lines that follow he also shifts the judgement: Petrarch hopes to find pity 'wherever there is anyone who understands love through experience' ('ove sia chi per prova intenda amore'), which Charlemont turns into 'if e'er their hearts for love have bled'.

anchor: Not only pardon, but perhaps a tear
title: pardon... a tear
short: Renders 'spero trovar pietà, nonché perdono': the poet hopes for pity, not merely pardon; Charlemont's 'tear' stands for pietà.
body: The Italian 'nonché' has been read in two ways: as 'not only... but also' (pity as well as pardon) or as 'let alone' (pity, to say nothing of pardon). Most modern editors take it in the first, rising sense, which Charlemont also follows: readers who have loved will not just forgive but sympathise. His 'tear' concretises pietà, a key word in Petrarch, meaning both compassion and the piety of fellow-feeling. The octave thus closes on a hope of shared feeling, which the sestet then undercuts with shame.

title: the turn (volta)
short: The sestet opens with 'Ma ben veggio or', the turn from the past of love to the present of self-judgement.
body: Petrarch's sonnet hinges at line 9, as the Italian form normally does: the octave addresses readers and hopes for sympathy; the sestet turns to what the poet now 'sees', that he has been a public joke, and moves to shame, repentance and a final general truth. The 'now' ('or') sets the whole collection in retrospect. Charlemont keeps the turn at the same point and the same 'now', and keeps the sestet rhyme CDECDE (mankind, thought, teem; find, dear-bought, dream).

anchor: Long time I was the tale
title: the tale of mankind
greek: favola fui gran tempo; Lat. fabula quanta fui
short: Petrarch's 'favola fui gran tempo' echoes Horace's 'fabula quanta fui', 'what a byword I was', in Epode 11.
body: Petrarch writes that he was for a long time 'the talk of all the people' ('al popol tutto / favola fui gran tempo'). Commentators point to Horace, Epodes 11.7-8, where the lover laments 'fabula quanta fui', ashamed at being gossiped about through Rome. Biblical idiom offers a parallel: the psalmist is made 'a byword among the heathen' (Psalm 44:14). Charlemont's 'of mankind / Long time I was the tale' keeps the double sense of 'tale': a story told and an object of mockery.

title: self-reproach... blushes
greek: di me medesmo meco mi vergogno
short: Petrarch's 'di me medesmo meco mi vergogno' (I am ashamed of myself within myself) is famous for its piled-up first-person forms.
body: The Italian line repeats the sounds of 'me' (me medesmo meco mi), enacting a self turned in on itself. Shame (vergogna) is felt privately as well as publicly. Charlemont cannot reproduce the sound play and translates it into a visible symptom, 'frequent blushes', paired with 'bitter thought / And self-reproach'. The word vergogna returns in the next line, so shame is both the feeling and the 'fruit' of the past.

title: shame the fruit
short: Renders 'et del mio vaneggiar vergogna è 'l frutto'; commentators compare St Paul's question about the fruit of things now shameful.
body: Vaneggiar means to rave or to pursue vanities; Charlemont's 'frenzy' takes the first sense. The image of shame as the 'fruit' of past conduct recalls Romans 6:21: 'What fruit had ye then in those things whereof ye are now ashamed? for the end of those things is death.' The Pauline background suits the poem's penitential frame, and the word vaneggiar prepares for the Ecclesiastes-like close. Charlemont adds 'sad repentance' and 'the proof, dear-bought', expanding Petrarch's 'e 'l pentersi, e 'l conoscer chiaramente' (repentance, and knowing clearly).

title: the world's joy a dream
short: Translates 'che quanto piace al mondo è breve sogno': whatever pleases in the world is a brief dream.
body: The closing sententia states the moral of the whole book, in the spirit of Ecclesiastes ('vanity of vanities; all is vanity', 1:2) and of the vanitas tradition that Petrarch develops again in the Triumphs. Charlemont's 'flitting dream' renders 'breve sogno' well, but his 'the world's joy' narrows 'quanto piace al mondo' ('all that pleases in the world'), which includes Laura herself. Critics have long noted the tension: the proem condemns the love that the rest of the collection celebrates with such care.
